extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, regulators, advocacy groups, journalists, and the general public
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and findings about detecting, preventing, and remedying fraudulent or fake public comments submitted to government rulemakings (focused on the FCC 2017 net neutrality proceeding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy groups must obtain valid consent before submitting comments on someone's behalf
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocacy groups to take steps to ensure they have obtained valid consent from an individual before submitting a comment or message to the government on their behalf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires affirmative, verifiable consent procedures before submitting comments for others; avoids submitting comments based on purported consents obtained by lead generators. Anti-patterns include claiming consent when responses were fabricated or when individuals were unaware their identities were used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies and legislatures should hold advocacy groups and vendors accountable for submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies and legislatures that manage electronic systems that receive comments and messages to hold advocacy groups and their vendors more accountable for the comments they submit on behalf of individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impose oversight, reporting, and potential sanctions on organizations and third‑party vendors that submit bulk or third‑party comments. Accountability can include auditing vendor practices, requiring documentation of consent, and disallowing submissions where provenance cannot be verified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawmakers should strengthen laws to deter deceptive and unauthorized submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawmakers to strengthen laws to deter the submission of deceptive and unauthorized comments to the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative solutions may include clearer prohibitions on impersonation and astroturfing, civil and criminal penalties, disgorgement, and statutory tools to deter mass fraudulent campaigns. The report cites monetary penalties as part of enforcement (e.g., over $4.4 million in penalties/disgorgement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agencies should adopt technical safeguards against unauthorized bulk automation
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies to adopt technical safeguards to protect against unauthorized bulk submissions using automation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical measures can include rate‑limiting, CAPTCHAs or equivalent bot mitigations, stronger identity verification for bulk submissions, anomaly detection, and other automated submission filters to prevent or flag mass automated uploads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require transparency and prohibit astroturfing (disguising paid campaigns as grassroots)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disguising an orchestrated, paid campaign as a grassroots effort, to create a false appearance of genuine, unpaid public support — often referred to as astroturfing — is deceptive and should be countered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should require disclosure of funding and industry involvement in mass advocacy campaigns; submissions coordinated and paid for by industry should not be presented as independent public opinion. Enforcement should address covert, paid campaigns that create false impressions of public support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit impersonation and fabrication of consumer responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead generators and vendors must not fabricate consumers’ responses or impersonate real people when submitting comments and messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions that impersonate individuals (creating comments in a real person's name without authorization) are fraudulent. Systems and enforcement should detect impersonation and remove or refuse such comments; vendors found fabricating responses should face sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and investigate large‑scale anomalies (fictitious identities, single-actor/automated submissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The investigation identified millions of fake comments: ~8.5M impersonating real people and ~9.3M using fictitious identities, including most submitted by a single person using automated software.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitoring and forensic analysis should look for patterns indicative of fraud — e.g., huge volumes from a single account or IP, repeated or identical content, fictitious identity markers, or evidence of automated tools — and trigger further investigation or exclusion of those submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforce remedies: require comprehensive reforms by responsible firms and monetary penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreements with responsible lead generators (Fluent, Opt‑Intelligence, React2Media) require the companies to adopt comprehensive reforms in future advocacy campaigns and pay more than $4.4 million in penalties and disgorgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory and enforcement responses should include binding corrective measures (changes in business practices), monitoring/oversight of future campaigns, and monetary penalties to deter repeat behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using prizes/sweepstakes/giveaways to solicit comments without verifying authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead generators used prizes — like gift cards and sweepstakes entries — to lure consumers to their websites and join campaigns; many hired generators instead fabricated responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Soliciting comments via incentives creates risk of inauthentic participation and should be accompanied by strict verification of identity and consent; agencies or advocacy groups should avoid or tightly regulate incentive-based mass recruitment for comment campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit/monitor reuse of third‑party lead generators with histories of fraud across campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Three of the lead generation firms involved in the net neutrality campaigns had worked on more than 100 other, unrelated campaigns and engaged in fraud across many advocacy efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies, advocacy groups, and clients should vet and avoid contracting with lead generators that have demonstrated patterns of fraudulent behavior; procurement and engagement policies should include past‑conduct checks and termination clauses for fraud.
